identification.summary: Zigzag Hail is Microsoft's current name for the group long tracked publicly as Darkhotel, with DUBNIUM as the legacy Microsoft element name [S11][S10]. MITRE describes Darkhotel as a suspected South Korean threat group that has targeted victims primarily in East Asia since at least 2004, named for espionage against traveling executives via hotel Internet networks, and also using spearphishing and peer-to-peer file-sharing infection [S10]. Kaspersky's November 2014 report tied offensive activity to hotel and business-center Wi-Fi and physical connections, with some P2P distribution and spear-phishing [S1].
identification.firstObserved: MITRE: since at least 2004 [S10]. Kaspersky: malware (Tapaoux) appearing as early as 2007 [S1]. The two sources differ on start date.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Zigzag Hail (formerly DUBNIUM) [S11]. Thales tracks the same actor as ATK52 / APT-C-06 and says some analysts link it to North Korea because of overlap with ATK4, but the consensus points to South Korea [S9]. APT-C-60 is listed by Microsoft's mapping as an alias of this group [S11]; ESET separately describes APT-C-60 as a South Korea-aligned group [S6]. None of the sources retrieved here explain the basis for merging APT-C-60 with Darkhotel, so treat that overlap as a vendor-mapping claim to validate (see gaps).

attribution.sponsor: No government sponsor is named in the sources gathered. MITRE calls Darkhotel a suspected South Korean group [S10]; Thales states the consensus points to South Korea rather than North Korea [S9].
attribution.confidence: Low to moderate and vendor-assessed only. Dark Reading, reporting Kaspersky, described the actor as appearing Korean-speaking [S2]. ESET describes APT-C-60 as South Korea-aligned (some coverage notes the wording is tentative) [S6][S7]. No government attribution was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Language indicators reported by Kaspersky [S2]; vendor consensus summarized by Thales, including the minority view of North Korea links [S9]; MITRE ATT&CK group description [S10].

objectives: Espionage. Thales describes targeting of government entities, especially diplomatic, defense and law-enforcement, mainly for espionage [S9]. Kaspersky described targeting of senior executives (CEOs, sales and marketing directors, R&D staff) traveling in Asia-Pacific [S2].

sectors: Corporate executives and R&D staff traveling in Asia-Pacific [S2]
Government, diplomatic, defense and law enforcement [S9]
Hospitality (hotels as access vector; Macao resorts) [S5]
regions: 2015 victims listed by Kaspersky: North Korea, Russia, South Korea, Japan, Bangladesh, Thailand, India, Mozambique, Germany [S3]
Macao (2021-2022 hotel campaign, Trellix moderate-confidence attribution) [S5]
targeting.notes: Targeting is selective: Kaspersky noted that only a few hotel guests received the malicious package [S1]. The APT-C-60 targeting entries rest on the Microsoft alias mapping [S11] and should be validated.

capabilities.summary: Hotel and business-center network compromise delivering trojanized software-update installers masquerading as Google Toolbar, Adobe Flash and Windows Messenger, signed with forged digital certificates [S1]. Also spear-phishing with Flash and Internet Explorer zero-day exploits and nuclear-energy or weapons-themed lures, and large RAR archives distributed over P2P networks [S4]. In 2015 Kaspersky reported the group may have used a Flash zero-day leaked in the Hacking Team breach [S3]. Later Inexsmar activity (from September 2016 per Bitdefender) targeted political figures [S4]. APT-C-60 activity exploited WPS Office CVE-2024-7262 to deliver the SpyGlace backdoor [S6][S7], and used Google Drive, Bitbucket and StatCounter with a job-application lure and a VHDX/LNK chain against a Japanese organization [S8]. ATT&CK technique and software detail is in the MITRE group record [S10].

campaigns.name: Darkhotel hotel Wi-Fi campaign
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reports espionage against traveling executives in luxury Asian hotels using fake software-update prompts on hotel networks; only a few guests received the payload.

campaigns.name: Hacking Team Flash exploit use
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reports spear-phishing links to Flash exploits first seen in 2014, then from early July a switch to a zero-day that surfaced after the Hacking Team breach.

campaigns.name: Inexsmar
campaigns.summary: Bitdefender (via Security Affairs coverage, July 2017) reports an Inexsmar campaign dating to September 2016 that targeted political figures rather than corporate R&D staff.

campaigns.name: Macao luxury resort campaign
campaigns.summary: Trellix attributed a Macao hotel-focused campaign to Darkhotel with moderate confidence, citing a reused C2 IP address, matching targets and familiar C2 patterns.

campaigns.name: APT-C-60 WPS Office zero-day (CVE-2024-7262)
campaigns.summary: ESET reports a South Korea-aligned group exploited a WPS Office for Windows flaw via the ksoqing:// protocol handler and MHTML spreadsheets to deliver SpyGlace against East Asian targets; a second flaw, CVE-2024-7263, was found in analysis.

campaigns.name: APT-C-60 job-application lure against Japan
campaigns.summary: Coverage of JPCERT/CC analysis reports an August 2024 intrusion at a Japanese organization using a job-application email, a VHDX with decoy document and LNK, and abuse of Google Drive, Bitbucket and StatCounter to deliver SpyGlace.

diamond.adversary: Suspected Korean-speaking espionage actor; South Korea is the consensus attribution, North Korea a minority view; no state sponsor confirmed [S2][S9][S10].
diamond.capability: Trojanized update installers with forged certificates, Flash and IE zero-days, P2P-distributed archives, Hacking Team-derived exploit, Inexsmar, SpyGlace via WPS Office exploit [S1][S3][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised hotel Wi-Fi and login portals [S1][S2]; reused C2 IP in the Macao campaign [S5]; legitimate services (Google Drive, Bitbucket, StatCounter) in 2024 APT-C-60 activity [S8].
diamond.victim: Traveling executives and R&D staff, government and defense personnel, political figures, hotel guests in Asia-Pacific, Japanese organizations [S2][S4][S8][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on business and government targets in East Asia; Korean-peninsula context suggested by victim lists that include North Korea [S3][S9].
diamond.technology: Hotel and public Wi-Fi, software-update trust, Flash/IE and office-suite (WPS Office) vulnerabilities, P2P file sharing, cloud and code-hosting services for staging [S1][S4][S6][S8].

gaps: Microsoft's primary Zigzag Hail / DUBNIUM publications (including the 2016 'Reverse engineering DUBNIUM' post cited by MITRE) were not retrieved; a search did not surface them.

Basis for Microsoft mapping APT-C-60 to this group is not stated in retrieved sources; ESET describes APT-C-60 separately [S6]. Vendor cluster boundaries (Darkhotel/APT-C-06, APT-C-60) may not be identical.
Start date conflict: MITRE says 2004, Kaspersky 2007 [S1][S10].
No government attribution; South Korea vs North Korea link (ATK4 overlap) is unresolved [S9].

Original reports (Kaspersky PDF, Bitdefender, Trellix, ESET, JPCERT/CC) could not be fetched; claims rest on search-result summaries and secondary coverage. Source dates for S3 and S5 are approximate.
Zscaler 'new Darkhotel attack chain' reporting appeared in search results but was not read.
Current (2025-2026) activity under the Zigzag Hail name is not documented in sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Hotel and commercial lodging networks, business-center PCs, and Wi-Fi at travel locations are key terrain for personnel on temporary duty or visiting Asia-Pacific [S1][S2]. STEP 2: The actor selects few guests per hotel, so exposure is individual and hard to detect at the enterprise level [S1]. STEP 3: Template is network-positioned fake software update or spear-phish with zero-day, then backdoor and data collection; recent variants use office-suite exploits and cloud services for staging [S1][S4][S6][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against traveling executives, officials and East Asian government or defense personnel. MDCOA is use of a newly leaked or purchased zero-day against allied personnel during a regional crisis [S3]. Candidate indicators: update prompts on hotel captive portals, forged-certificate installers, ksoqing:// handler abuse, VHDX/LNK attachments, and traffic to Bitbucket or StatCounter from unusual hosts [S1][S6][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: share travel schedules and lodging locations with cyber defenders so hotel-network risk can be assessed [S1]. (2) Authorities: personal and commercial device use on lodging networks falls to local command and travel policy, not network operators, so require guidance on VPN use and no software updates on hotel networks [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: treat travelers' devices as untrusted on return and reimage or scan before reconnecting. (4) Coordination: because attribution (South Korea vs North Korea) and the APT-C-60 mapping are contested, route reporting through the intelligence lead and allied partners rather than naming a sponsor [S9][S11].

provenance.importedSummary: Darkhotel is a suspected South Korean threat group that has targeted victims primarily in East Asia since at least 2004. The group's name is based on cyber espionage operations conducted via hotel Internet networks against traveling executives and other select guests. Darkhotel has also conducted spearphishing campaigns and infected victims through peer-to-peer and file sharing networks.
